title: Testing the rapamycin–mTOR hypothesis in NF1 cells

sentences.text: This is a hypothesis, not a finding; its weakest link is the connection between the NF1 gene and TOR (mTOR) signaling.
Test whether rapamycin (sirolimus) changes an mTOR signaling readout in NF1-deficient cells.
The cited NF1 evidence describes constitutive mTOR activation in NF1-deficient primary cells in the absence of growth factors.
Use that cell context as the starting point; the lab would need to establish a usable model and signaling assay before testing.
Check the cited studies for a suitable readout rather than inventing an assay or assuming one is ready to use.
Measure the same selected mTOR signaling readout before and after rapamycin exposure, comparing treated and untreated cells.
Include NF1-deficient cells without rapamycin, keeping the assay conditions otherwise matched.

sections.heading: What result would change the plan

sentences.text: A reproducible reduction in the signaling readout would support further bench testing, not establish disease benefit.
No effect in a working assay would argue against pursuing this hypothesis in that model.
The graph contains no study, case report or model result testing this therapy class in NF1-related disorders.
Rapamycin reversed cardiac defects in LS/+ mice in the cited evidence, but that is not an NF1 result.
